results.content:
Title: Rebooting reproducibility: From re-execution to replication | Labs | eLife
Computational reproducibility should be trivial but it is not. The new solutions leverage software containers and follow a familiar pattern of standardization, simplification and automation to decrease mistakes and confusion, thereby improving the “user-friendliness” and robustness of computational reproducibility. Asking and answering these questions will hopefully initiate a new discussion around improving the quality and reproducibility of research, the user experience of peer review, and the practical and economic realities of computational reproducibility. An individual’s motivations around computational reproducibility determine their standards and approach, but regardless of the definition (see a good one in The Turing Way), reproducibility is an important proxy for something much more difficult: replicability. Community-based demands for reproducibility make it easier to subject the author’s work (and the journal’s review process) to knowledgeable and competitive scrutiny, significantly reducing the difficulty and time required to understand and then accept or challenge the results. Prioritizing ease of interrogation and reuse in computational reproducibility preferences a dynamic type of reproducibility that merges into replicability, wherein the techniques producing a specific result are intelligible, re-executable and extendable to novel data or computational techniques. Defining ease as minimizing the amount of time, skill and money is reasonable, but it depends on the computation and whoever is trying to reproduce it. In the figure, the line indicates where the majority of time, skill and money would be spent to reproduce computations. Reproducing computations on the left-hand side is “difficult” while reproducing those on the right-hand side is “easy”, i.e. there are existing solutions that significantly reduce the time, skill and money to reproduce them. Large data, specialized hardware and long compute times make such workflows difficult or infeasible to reproduce. ###### The dotted line is a practical division between computations that are difficult to reproduce and those that are easy or feasible in this toy model. We also need models to help evaluate reproducibility solutions themselves. The evaluation rubric represents what we’ve prioritized in our approach in trying to understand and tackle “difficult” reproducibility problems – moving further to the left side of our diagram where expensive (and energy-intensive) compute meets ever-increasing quantities of data.

results.title: Embedding model evaluation into CI_CD pipelines
results.content: Embedding model evaluation into CI_CD pipelines – The Palos Publishing Company Embedding model evaluation into CI_CD pipelines Embedding model evaluation into CI/CD pipelines is a critical practice to ensure machine learning models maintain their quality, performance, and reliability over time. Similarly, integrating model evaluation into CI/CD helps teams efficiently monitor model performance, track changes, and detect potential issues that may arise during updates. Here’s how to effectively embed model evaluation into CI/CD pipelines: ### 1. **Automate Data Preprocessing and Model Training** The first step of any machine learning pipeline is data preprocessing, which includes cleaning, transforming, and preparing data for model training. By automating this process in your CI/CD pipeline, you ensure that your model gets consistently trained with the latest version of your data. **Integrate Evaluation Step Post-Training** Once the model has been trained, it’s crucial to evaluate its performance against a validation set. This step is a key part of the CI/CD pipeline, as it helps detect whether the model’s performance meets the established benchmarks. * **Model Evaluation**: After model training, use the defined evaluation metrics to measure performance against the validation or test dataset. This ensures that each version of the model can be traced back to a specific set of evaluation results and allows for reproducibility of training and testing. **Model Performance Monitoring in Production** After deploying a model, continuous evaluation doesn’t stop. * **Real-time Evaluation**: Implement real-time scoring and logging of model predictions to track performance on live data. Incorporating model rollback mechanisms into the CI/CD pipeline is crucial. * **Rollback Triggers**: Define the conditions under which the pipeline should revert to an earlier model version, such as performance degradation or failed tests. Create a step in the CI/CD pipeline that specifically tests the model for robustness against these issues. ### Conclusion Integrating model evaluation into CI/CD pipelines helps ensure that machine learning models are consistently performing at their best, while also allowing teams to quickly detect and respond to performance degradation. Through automated testing, continuous monitoring, and version control, organizations can effectively manage their machine learning models in production, reduce manual oversight, and deliver reliable AI solutions.
